tips.title: Sur for online places
tips.body: French uses **sur** for being *on* a device or site: *sur mon portable, sur Internet, sur les réseaux sociaux, sur YouTube*. English says *on* too, so this one is easy — but *en ligne* is *online* as an adjective or adverb: *je suis en ligne, un jeu en ligne*.

tips.title: Passer + time = how long you spend
tips.body: *Je **passe** deux heures **par jour** sur mon portable.* *Passer* with a length of time and *par jour / par semaine* is how French says how long you spend doing something. It is a present tense -er verb and a whole answer in one sentence.

tips.title: The -ger verbs keep their e
tips.body: *Partager, télécharger, échanger* are regular -er verbs with one rule: the **nous** form keeps the **e** to stay soft — *nous partag**e**ons, nous télécharg**e**ons*. Like *mangeons*. Everywhere else they are ordinary.

tips.title: Give the dangers a verb
tips.body: A point about online safety needs a full sentence: *il ne faut pas donner son mot de passe*, *c'est dangereux de parler à des inconnus*. **Il faut / il ne faut pas** + infinitive is the structure, and it is worth a mark on its own.

tips.title: Trop de means too much
tips.body: *Je passe **trop de** temps en ligne.* *Trop de* + noun is *too much / too many*, and it is the natural way into a balanced opinion: what you like about life online, then what there is too much of.

why.matters: What you do online is the easiest French you will ever produce, because it is all regular *-er* verbs in the present: *je poste, je partage, je regarde, je télécharge*. The topic exists to attach the small words to them, *sur* for where, *en ligne* for being online, *passer* with a time for how long, and to practise the shrinking of *des* to *de* after a negative, *je ne poste jamais de photos*, which is one of the clearest signs of control in a Year 9 answer. It also opens the for-and-against shape that the technology topic next year needs.

examples.title: Two hours a day is fourteen a week
examples.body: *Je passe deux heures par jour sur mon portable* sounds modest until it is multiplied: two hours a day is 14 hours a week, and the arithmetic is the kind of point a balanced paragraph can make. *Passer* takes the time and *par jour* or *par semaine* follows it, and the number is the detail a listening question asks for. Say the small figure, then the large one, and the opinion about screens writes itself.

examples.title: Sur mon portable
examples.body: Where online life happens is always *sur*: *sur mon portable, sur ma tablette, sur Internet, sur les réseaux sociaux*. English *on* and French *sur* match here, which is a rare gift, and *dans* in any of these reads as translated. Being online is *être en ligne*, and *Internet* takes no article at all. Four phrases, and the whole vocabulary of where you spend your evenings is in place.

steps.title: Ce que je fais en ligne
steps.body:
Talking about life online is talking about **what you do**, so it runs on **-er verbs** in the present tense — exactly the pattern from the present tense topic, with a new set of verbs.

*Je **poste** des photos. Je **tchatte** avec mes amis. Je **regarde** des vidéos. Je **joue** à des jeux vidéo. Je **télécharge** de la musique. Je **partage** des vidéos.*

Each is *je* + stem + **-e**, and each takes an object with its article — *des photos, des vidéos, de la musique*.

**Where it happens** takes **sur**: *sur mon portable, sur ma tablette, sur Internet, sur les réseaux sociaux*. English *on* and French *sur* match here.

**Being online** is *être en ligne*: *je suis en ligne tous les soirs*. *En ligne* also describes things: *un jeu en ligne, un ami en ligne*.

**The kit** is mostly cognates or near-cognates: *un portable* (mobile), *un smartphone*, *une tablette*, *un ordinateur* (computer), *une appli* (app), *un réseau social* (social network), *un mot de passe* (password), *un site web*.

steps.title: Combien de temps ?
steps.body:
The question a text or a speaking examiner asks is **how much** — how often, and how long.

**How long**: *passer* + a length of time + *par jour / par semaine*. *Je passe **deux heures par jour** sur mon portable.* That is 2 hours a day, so 14 hours a week — the kind of figure a text may ask you to work out.

*Une demi-heure* is half an hour, *une heure* an hour, *trois heures* three hours. *Environ* (about) softens a number: *environ trois heures*.

**How often**: the frequency words from the present tense topic — *tous les jours, tous les soirs, souvent, quelquefois, rarement, ne … jamais*. *Je tchatte tous les soirs. Je ne poste jamais de photos.*

**Note *jamais de*.** After a negative, *des* becomes **de**: *je ne poste jamais **de** photos*, *je n'envoie pas **de** messages*. The article shrinks after *ne … pas* and *ne … jamais*.

**When**: *le soir* (in the evening), *le matin*, *après l'école*, *avant de dormir* (before sleeping), *pendant le week-end*.

steps.title: Pour et contre
steps.body:
Every opinion about life online has two sides, and the exam expects you to give both.

**Advantages**: *c'est pratique* (handy), *c'est rapide*, *on peut rester en contact avec ses amis*, *on peut faire des recherches pour l'école*, *on peut regarder des vidéos gratuitement*.

**Disadvantages**: *on passe trop de temps en ligne*, *c'est mauvais pour les yeux*, *on ne dort pas assez*, *il y a des inconnus* (strangers), *c'est dangereux si on donne ses informations*.

**Advice** uses **il faut** and **il ne faut pas** + infinitive: *il faut faire attention*, *il ne faut pas parler à des inconnus*, *il ne faut jamais donner son mot de passe*. *Il faut* is impersonal — it never changes for the person — which makes it one of the easiest structures to get right.

**Trop de / assez de / beaucoup de** + noun: *trop de temps* (too much time), *beaucoup de photos* (lots of photos), *pas assez de sommeil* (not enough sleep). The **de** never becomes *du* or *des* after a quantity.

**Balancing it**: *d'un côté … de l'autre côté* (on one hand… on the other), *mais*, *par contre*, *cependant* (however).

steps.title: Your turn
steps.body:
**Part A.**

1. List four things you do online, each with a present tense verb.
2. Translate: *I chat with my friends every evening.*
3. How do you say *online* in French?

**Part B.**

4. Say how long you spend on your phone each day, with *passer*.
5. Write *I never send messages* — watch the article.
6. Give one advantage and one disadvantage of social networks.

**Part C.**

7. Write a piece of safety advice using *il ne faut pas*.
8. Write the nous form of *télécharger* and explain its spelling.
9. Write five sentences about your online life: what, how often, how long, an opinion with a reason, and a disadvantage.

For question 9, use *sur* for where and *de* after any negative.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Use sur, and en ligne, correctly.** *Sur mon portable, sur Internet, sur les réseaux sociaux* — and *je suis en ligne*. Mixing *dans* in here reads as translated English.

**Shrink the article after a negative.** *Je ne poste jamais **de** photos, je n'envoie pas **de** messages.* *Des* becomes *de* after *ne … pas* and *ne … jamais*. It is one of the clearest signs of control in a Year 9 answer.

**Quantify.** *Je passe environ deux heures par jour…*, *trop de temps*, *beaucoup de photos*. Numbers and quantities are detail the examiner can tick, and *passer + time* is a whole sentence structure in itself.

**Keep the e in the -ger nous forms.** *Nous partageons, nous téléchargeons, nous échangeons.* The rule is the same as *mangeons*, and a piece of writing with a correct *-geons* shows you know it.

**Balance the opinion.** Advantages with *on peut…*, disadvantages with *trop de… / c'est dangereux…*, joined by *d'un côté… de l'autre* or *par contre*. A balanced answer gives you more to say, and justifying opinions is part of what the speaking and writing papers assess.

**Give advice with il faut.** *Il faut faire attention, il ne faut pas parler à des inconnus.* Impersonal, never conjugated for a person, followed by an infinitive — easy to get right and always relevant to this topic.

**Extend with pour + infinitive.** *J'utilise mon portable **pour** tchatter et **pour** faire des recherches.* *Pour* + infinitive says what something is for, and turns a list of verbs into purposes.

**Do not conjugate after pouvoir, falloir or pour.** *On peut regarder, il faut faire, pour tchatter* — the infinitive every time.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- Online activities are **-er verbs**: *poster, tchatter, partager, télécharger, regarder, jouer*.
- **Sur** for where: *sur mon portable, sur Internet, sur les réseaux sociaux*.
- **En ligne** = online: *je suis en ligne*.
- **Passer** + time + **par jour**: *je passe deux heures par jour…*
- 2 hours a day is **14** hours a week.
- Frequency: *tous les soirs, souvent, ne … jamais*.
- After a negative, **des → de**: *je ne poste jamais de photos*.
- **-ger** verbs keep the **e** in *nous*: *partageons, téléchargeons*.
- Advantages: *pratique, rapide, on peut rester en contact*.
- Disadvantages: *trop de temps, dangereux, des inconnus*.
- **Il faut / il ne faut pas** + infinitive for advice.
- **Trop de, beaucoup de, pas assez de** + noun.
- Balance with *d'un côté … de l'autre*, *par contre*.
- **Pour** + infinitive says what you use it for.
- Infinitives after *pouvoir, falloir* and *pour*.

examTechnique.body:
Use **sur** for where and **en ligne** for online. Quantify with **passer + time + par jour** and the frequency words, and shrink **des to de** after any negative.

Give **both sides** of the opinion, joined by *d'un côté … de l'autre*, and add advice with **il (ne) faut (pas)** + infinitive. Keep the **e** in *partageons*.
examinerErrors: Writing dans Internet instead of sur Internet.
Dropping the e in the nous form of -ger verbs.
Conjugating the verb after il faut.
Using a list of verbs with no pour + infinitive.
Forgetting the article after opinion verbs.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer places every activity **sur** the right device, quantifies it with **passer + time**, and shrinks the article to **de** after a negative without a second thought. It balances the opinion — *d'un côté … de l'autre* — with a reason on each side, and closes with advice built on **il ne faut pas** + infinitive. It uses **pour** + infinitive to turn a list into purposes, keeps the **e** in *partageons*, and never conjugates after *pouvoir*, *falloir* or *pour*.
